1:
The date is fixed by the king's death rather than the birth. Ellicott sets that death just before a Passover in a year answering to four before the common era, and concludes that our ordinary reckoning is wrong and the Nativity earlier than the numbering suggests; on the season he says only that flocks in the open field point to spring rather than winter. Henry marks the obscurity as deliberate, that one who was the desire of all nations came into the world unregarded, having emptied himself and made himself of no reputation.

The star is where the fathers are most careful. Chrysostom argues that it was manifestly not one of the common stars, since none moves as this did, from east to south, which is the lie of Palestine with respect to Persia; and he turns the astrological reading around, since the art is used not to learn a birth from the stars but to forecast a life from its hour, whereas these men did the converse. Gregory names the party he argues with, heretics who hold every man born under the aspect of some planet and cite this very text for it; far be it, he answers, from the hearts of the faithful to call anything fate, since prayer is vain for men who live by it, and providence is banished along with piety when man is made the instrument of the motions of the sky. Robertson thinks the words about the east go with the seeing rather than the star, so they saw it at its rising.

Three of them describe the king from the histories. Robertson recalls what anyone who knows Josephus will remember, a man who had put to death two sons by his best-loved wife, that wife herself, another son once his heir, and her brother and mother. Ellicott adds the timing, an old reign drawing to its blood-stained close and the eldest son under condemnation as this history opens. Leo addresses the man directly: his alarm is groundless, since his nature cannot contain Christ and the Lord of the world is not content with the narrow bounds of one dominion. Augustine sets the parties against each other in a sentence, that the Magi seek a Redeemer while Herod fears a successor, and asks what the tribunal of the Judge will do if the cradle already makes proud kings tremble. Gregory reduces it further, that when heavenly greatness shows itself earthly greatness is confounded.

Augustine also notices what the star did not do: it could have conducted them straight to the town, and instead vanished and did not show itself again until the Jews themselves had named the place.

On the council Lightfoot cautions about a story often repeated, that this king is said by very many authors to have slain the Sanhedrim, which he holds must not be understood of the whole body nor taken for its abolition. Robertson doubts whether a formal assembly was called at all, since the question could as easily have been put to one leader after another, which the tense of the verb suggests.

The quotation from the prophet is treated as a problem of transmission. Ellicott points out that the Evangelist is not quoting it himself but recording how the scribes quoted it, which is why it follows neither the Greek version nor the Hebrew closely but a free paraphrase. Calvin draws a larger inference, that Matthew thought it enough to indicate the passage and followed the ordinary reading because he wrote in Greek, which tells against the notion that this Gospel was composed in Hebrew. Chrysostom presses the wording, that the prophet does not say the ruler shall be in Bethlehem but shall come out of it, which shows he was only to be born there.
7:
The secrecy of the summons is read as characteristic. Ellicott calls it true to his nature, a king probably himself a believer in astrology and haunted by what the star portended, whose next move is to measure his danger; he corrects the English too, since the question is not when the star appeared but when the star now visible had first done so. Robertson notes that the Sanhedrin had not been told why the birthplace mattered, so the motive is hidden from the Magi too. Calvin supplies the politics, that the tyrant dared not avow his fear lest it give fresh courage to a people he knew hated him.

On the pretended homage the comment is unanimous and unsparing. Clarke calls it exquisite hypocrisy, since the man wished only to find the child in order to murder him, and observes how the God who searches the heart defeats such designs. Barnes notes that the errand would have looked suspicious had it not been clothed in religion, and that the king had asked the exact time, reckoning the star had appeared at the birth; Robertson says the deceit was plausible enough to have worked but for the intervention that followed. Chrysostom catches what the wording gives away: the king says the young child and not the king, grudging him the title.

The star returns, and the accounts of it differ in kind. Lightfoot supposes it shone on the birth night and then disappeared, no guide being needed to a city as well known as Jerusalem, and reappeared for the road to Bethlehem. Barnes and Clarke take it for a luminous meteor at no great height, since it could not otherwise have marked the particular house; Robertson agrees that it guided them not to the town but to the place within it. Augustine describes the movement as service rather than mechanism: it advanced slowly to do its duty, ministering to the Lord and not ruling his fate, and its light filled the lodging before it went out.

Calvin is indignant at who did not go, calling it base sluggishness that not one Jew offered himself as escort to these foreigners, the scribes naming the place and then letting them depart alone, not a man moving a step.

The gifts are read both as custom and as sign. Clarke observes that in the east nobody approaches a king empty-handed, and reports without adopting the reading that makes the three stand for divinity, royal office and manhood. Ellicott compares the presents Jacob sent into Egypt, and notes that the word for treasures means the caskets they were carried in, as Robertson also says. Gregory gives the symbolic reading, gold to a king, frankincense in sacrifice to God, myrrh for embalming, and turns each into a duty, incense standing for prayer and myrrh for mortification. Wesley alone asks what the gifts were for, calling them a most seasonable and providential assistance toward a long and expensive journey into Egypt.

Leo and Chrysostom use the scene against later error. Leo observes that the child was in stature an infant, needing help and unable to speak and in nothing different from other children, so witnesses of this kind ought to have settled that the eternal Son had taken a true human nature. Chrysostom names two heretics and tells them to blush, since the swaddling clothes and the stall prove the flesh while the gifts prove that the worship was not offered to a mere man.

On the warning that sends them home another way, Chrysostom praises the obedience, that they did not ask what need there was of flight if this child were really some great one, true faith asking no reason for a command. Gregory turns the detour into an allegory of the return to Paradise, forbidden by the road we left it on, since we went out by pride and must come back by repentance.
13:
Henry notices the irony of the timing, that the flight is the direct result of the visit paid to the child, since until then the obscurity he lay in had been his protection; the little respect shown him in infancy did not honour him among his people but only exposed him. Chrysostom turns the same fact into consolation, that the tyrant rages against him from the moment of his birth and the mother is driven into a foreign country, so that a man who meets trouble at the beginning of his own spiritual course need not be discouraged but may bear it with this example before him. Calvin calls the method itself remarkable, that God chose to preserve his Son by flight, and supposes the order was delayed until the mother had recovered enough from childbirth to travel.

Why Egypt is answered from geography and from settlement. Barnes puts it some sixty miles off, a Roman province where Greek was spoken and where there were Jews enough to have a temple and synagogues, so that Joseph would be among his own countrymen and still beyond the reach of Herod's jurisdiction. Clarke and Lightfoot fill in how those Jews came to be there, some from the old flight under Jeremiah and many more drawn later by the temple built at Heliopolis, with Clarke adding that Greek-speakers had the advantage of the older Greek version to hand. Ellicott says only that the nearness of the country had always made it the natural refuge.

Two of the fathers refuse to let the flight be merely an escape. Augustine sets it against the older history: Moses had shut the light of day away from the Egyptians, and Christ by going down brought light back to those sitting in darkness, so that he fled in order to enlighten them and not in order to evade his enemies. Bede takes it as precedent rather than symbol, that the elect are often driven from their homes by the wickedness of others, and that the man who afterwards told his followers to flee from one city to another had first done himself what he enjoined.

Ellicott makes two observations about the telling. The phrase naming the child before the mother he calls significantly reverential, since in an ordinary narrative the natural order would have been the wife and then the child; and he finds in the sheer brevity of the account an argument, so far as it goes, against treating the story as myth.

The quotation from the prophet is the crux, and nobody pretends it is easy. Clarke states the difficulty without softening it: the words in their place refer to the deliverance of Israel and to nothing else, and his own suggestion is that so extraordinary a deliverance had passed into a proverb for any signal rescue; beyond that, he confesses he can see no other reference the words can have to the case in hand. Wesley solves it by the grammar, holding that the word rendered as purpose frequently signifies not the design of an action but merely its consequence, so that what is meant is that the saying was fulfilled anew, Christ being the Son of God in a far higher sense than Israel was. Chrysostom states the principle more broadly, that it is a law of prophecy for things to be said in one place of one subject and fulfilled in another of a different one. Calvin attacks a rival reading rather than the difficulty, saying that those who make the prophet mean something else grievously pervert his words, whose design was to establish a charge. Robertson says only that the evangelist quotes the prophet to show the application, and Ellicott keeps to chronology, that the king died a little before a Passover, so the stay in Egypt can have been only a few months.
16:
What the king thought he had suffered is distinguished from what happened. Barnes points out that the word does not mean the Magi set out to deride him, only that he was disappointed by their not returning, and that he had expected to send one executioner against one child. Wesley says his pride made him read the departure as designed to expose him to the derision of his subjects. Calvin puts it more sharply, that the evangelist reports what the man felt rather than what was true: he believed himself deceived by men who had merely refused to share his cruelty, and was in fact caught by his own trick, the pretence that he too meant to pay homage. Henry describes the waiting before the rage, a king hoping that visitors slow to return would still be sure, and growing suspicious that they had gone over to the new king's interest. Robertson explains the width of the order, that Herod had no way of knowing the child's age and therefore took in every boy rather than risk the one. Chrysostom will not call the state of mind anger, since the case called for fear and awe and the man ought to have seen he was attempting the impossible; but a soul past cure yields to none of the medicines God gives.

That no historian records the massacre is faced by three of them. Ellicott states the objection plainly, that neither Josephus nor any other writer mentions it and its historicity has been questioned on that ground, and answers that it is admitted on all hands to be entirely in keeping with the man's character, a king tormented by incurable disease and still more incurable suspicion. Calvin notes the same silence and names the one writer he knows who alludes to it. Clarke gives the allusion itself, from a Latin author of the fourth century, who reports the jest that it was better to be this king's pig than his son.

Lightfoot uses the age limit to date the episode, reckoning about two years since the star had shone, and explains why the family had stayed so long in one small town, supposing that a Messiah born there was to be brought up nowhere else.

Two of the fathers read the killing as a gain rather than only a loss. Augustine observes that in persecuting Christ the king unintentionally furnished an army of martyrs of the Lord's own age, and that this enemy could never have profited the children by his love as he did by his hate. Bede takes them for a figure of all Christ's martyrs and presses the details, that their infancy shows the glory of martyrdom reached by humility alone, and that their dying in Bethlehem and its borders foreshadows persecution both where the Church began and throughout the world.

The lament quoted from the prophet turns on a woman long dead. Calvin identifies what it originally described, the destruction of the tribe of Benjamin in the prophet's own day, and calls the device by its name, a personification that puts the mourning into the mouth of Rachel and has great power in moving the affections. Wesley works the same figure out, that the people of Ramah were descended from her and that she is represented as risen from her grave to bewail them, and glosses the closing words as meaning simply that they are dead. Barnes and Clarke supply the history behind it, the captives gathered at Ramah after the city fell, Clarke adding that Bethlehem at this hour resembled Ramah, weeping for children slaughtered as the other had wept for children carried away. Ellicott anchors it to the ground itself, since the tomb of Rachel stood on the road to the very town where the children died.
19:
Henry states the principle behind the return in a sentence: Egypt may serve to sojourn in or shelter in for a while but not to abide in, and one sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel must go back to them. Calvin reads the same interval as a test passed, that Joseph kept his feet firm abroad until a command recalled him, and takes it for evidence that the Lord never disappoints his own but sends help in season. Bede makes the sequence a figure, the slaughter, the persecutor's death soon after and the return together showing that persecutions against the Church end in the death of the persecutor, the restoring of peace, and the return of saints who had hidden themselves.

The plural in the message puzzles four of them, since only one man had been named. Barnes and Clarke suppose a second person is genuinely meant, the king's eldest son having been put to death by his father a few days before his own, and Clarke adds that this son had cleared his way to the throne by procuring the deaths of his elder brothers. Ellicott allows that others may have been implicated, but thinks the phrasing likelier suggested by the parallel words spoken to Moses. Robertson agrees and puts it as a habit of speech, a general statement covering a particular fact, of the kind people make when they say they say.

On the son who was now reigning the commentators supply what the narrative assumes. Clarke sets out the division under the will, Galilee and the country beyond Jordan to one son, the northern tetrarchy to another, Judea to the eldest then living. Robertson adds what makes the fear intelligible, that in a fit of temper before his death the old king had altered his will again and put the worst of his surviving sons in the place meant for another. Ellicott corrects the title, since this prince was never recognised as king by the emperor but held the lesser rank of ethnarch, the higher word surviving only in popular use. Barnes gives the character, a temper as cruel as his father's, three thousand men put to death at a single Passover, and banishment after nine years.

Augustine raises the difficulty this fear creates. If the family avoided Judea because of this ruler, how could they go up to Jerusalem every year of the childhood, as another Gospel relates? A festival crowd would hide them, he answers, and a short stay end the risk, so they could keep the feast without living where they dared not live.

The last quotation is the hardest in the chapter, because the words quoted are nowhere to be found. Robertson states the problem exactly: the evangelist writes prophets in the plural, and no single prophecy says the Messiah should be called by this name; he suggests the term of contempt is what is meant and that several prophecies are combined. Wesley puts it as a distinction, that the thing was spoken in effect by several of the prophets though in express words by none, and that to be called by this name is to be despised and rejected. Clarke admits he cannot tell which prophets are intended, and reports the two passages usually offered, the promise about the Nazarite at Samson's birth and the branch from the stem of Jesse. Lightfoot grants both have their weight and will dismiss neither, but takes the evangelist to be speaking of the outward and mean condition of the Saviour. Calvin will not have the second passage treated as an etymology at all, holding that the evangelist is making an allusion and not deriving one word from another. Barnes supplies the fact that gives the contempt its edge, that the town itself was proverbial for wickedness.
